questions.q: How does reconciliation relate to the consistency checks from Lesson 13?
options: Reconciliation scales the same comparison idea from a single row up to an aggregate across an entire dataset
Reconciliation only applies to text data, while consistency only applies to numeric data
Reconciliation replaces the need for consistency checks entirely
They are unrelated techniques that happen to use JOIN syntax
questions.explain: Consistency compares one row's value to its copy elsewhere; reconciliation compares an aggregate (count, sum) for a whole dataset between two systems that should agree — the same underlying question, scaled up.

questions.q: What does a count reconciliation check verify?
options: Whether two systems agree on how many records exist for a matching scope
Whether a column's values fall within an allowed range
Whether a specific row's value matches a trusted reference
Whether a table has any duplicate rows
questions.explain: Count reconciliation compares row counts (for a given date, batch, etc.) between two systems — a mismatch typically signals a failed load, a filtering bug, or a duplicated batch.

questions.q: Why can a sum reconciliation check fail even when a count reconciliation check for the same scope passes?
options: The right number of rows can still contain corrupted or mis-mapped individual values, which only a sum check would catch
Sum reconciliation and count reconciliation always produce identical results
SQL Server computes SUM() and COUNT() using different data types that can never agree
Count reconciliation is always run before sum reconciliation, making the sum check redundant
questions.explain: Matching row counts only confirm the same number of records exist — it says nothing about whether individual values (like OrderTotal) are correct. A sum check catches value-level discrepancies that a count check misses.

questions.q: What does a linked server allow in the context of reconciliation?
options: Querying a table on a separate SQL Server instance directly from within the same script
Automatically fixing mismatches found during reconciliation
Converting between different database engines like SQL Server and Oracle
Running a query without needing to connect to any server
questions.explain: A linked server lets a query reference a database on another SQL Server instance, which is necessary when reconciling data that lives in genuinely separate systems rather than two tables in the same database.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe a reconciliation mismatch as 'a symptom, not a diagnosis'?
options: It confirms two systems disagree but doesn't explain why or which side is correct — that's root cause analysis
Reconciliation checks are always false positives and should be ignored
A mismatch means the SQL query itself contains a syntax error
Reconciliation checks can only be run once per year
questions.explain: The lesson draws a clear line: reconciliation's job is reliably detecting disagreement; figuring out the actual cause and which side is correct is root cause analysis, covered in a later lesson.
